method_card.title: Tally Charts, Tabulation and Pictograms
method_card.content:
A tally chart is a quick way to count items as they occur. Each item is recorded with a vertical stroke; the fifth stroke is drawn diagonally across the previous four to form a bundle of five, making counting fast and accurate. Always group your tally marks into fives before reading totals.

A frequency table (or tabulation) organises data into categories with their corresponding frequencies. When data is numerical, it is grouped into class intervals — for example, “10 ≤ h < 20”. Each interval uses ≤ on the left and < on the right so that no value falls in two classes at once.

A pictogram uses a repeated symbol to represent data. The most important step is reading the key carefully: if one symbol represents 4 items, then half a symbol represents 2 items and a quarter symbol represents 1 item. The most common error at Foundation tier is ignoring the key and treating every symbol as worth 1.

When critiquing a diagram, look for these misrepresentation errors: a truncated axis (y-axis not starting at zero, which exaggerates differences), an incorrect scale (unequal gaps between tick marks), and distorted sizing (symbols at different sizes in a pictogram, or bar widths that vary). Any of these can mislead the reader about the size of differences in the data.

When choosing between formats: use a tally chart to collect live data; use a frequency table to present discrete or grouped data clearly; use a pictogram when the audience is non-specialist and the frequencies are whole multiples of the key value.
steps: Read the key on any pictogram before counting symbols
Multiply the number of complete symbols by the key value
For partial symbols, use the fraction shown (half symbol = half the key value)
Check a frequency table by summing all frequencies to get the total
Identify misrepresentation by checking whether the axis starts at zero and the scale is even
State why the misrepresentation is misleading, not just that it exists

exam_context.marks: 1–4 marks per question; pictogram reading is typically 1–2 marks, table completion up to 4 marks
exam_context.frequency: At least one tally/table/pictogram question appears on every paper; pictogram key errors are the single most common Foundation 1-mark drop

worked_examples.question: A pictogram shows the number of books read by students in a week. The key states: one symbol = 4 books. One student's row shows 3 complete symbols and one half symbol. How many books did that student read?

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the key
steps.content: Each complete symbol = 4 books. A half symbol = 2 books.

steps.label: Step 2 — Count and multiply
steps.content: 3 complete symbols: \(3 \times 4 = 12\) books. Half symbol: \(0.5 \times 4 = 2\) books.

worked_examples.question: A frequency table shows the scores of 40 students on a quiz: Score 1–10: 8 students; Score 11–20: 14 students; Score 21–30: frequency missing; Score 31–40: 7 students. Find the missing frequency.

A bar chart showing monthly rainfall has its y-axis starting at 20 mm rather than 0 mm. The bar for June reaches 30 mm and the bar for July reaches 60 mm. A student claims July had three times as much rainfall as June. Explain whether this is correct.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the true values
steps.content: Both bars must be read from zero, not from the truncated axis origin. June = 30 mm; July = 60 mm.

steps.label: Step 2 — Calculate the true ratio
steps.content: \(\frac{60}{30} = 2\). July had twice as much rainfall, not three times.

steps.label: Step 3 — Explain the misrepresentation
steps.content: The truncated axis makes the bar for July appear three times the height of June's bar on the chart, but the actual values show only a two-fold difference. The student is incorrect because they read the visual bar heights rather than the true values from zero.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The student is wrong. The truncated axis exaggerates the visual difference. The true rainfall ratio is 2:1, not 3:1.

bronze.display: A pictogram uses one football to represent 6 goals. A team's row shows 4 complete footballs. How many goals did the team score?

misconceptions.message: Read the key first: 1 symbol = 6 goals. 4 symbols = 4 × 6 = 24 goals. Do not count each symbol as 1.

bronze.display: A pictogram uses one apple to represent 8 items. A row shows 2 complete apples and one half apple. How many items does this represent?

misconceptions.message: 2 complete = 2 × 8 = 16. Half apple = 0.5 × 8 = 4. Total = 16 + 4 = 20.
Don’t forget to include the half symbol: it represents half the key value, which is 4 here.

bronze.display: A tally chart shows: | = 1, |||| = 4, ||||  | = 6. How many items are tallied in total?

misconceptions.message: Count each group: 1 + 4 + 6 = 11. The diagonal stroke in a group of 5 is the fifth stroke, not an extra.

bronze.display: A frequency table has four categories with frequencies 12, 9, 15, and 4. What is the total frequency?

misconceptions.message: Add all frequencies: 12 + 9 + 15 + 4 = 40. Do not count the number of categories.

bronze.display: A pictogram shows 3 complete symbols and one quarter symbol. The key is: 1 symbol = 20 items. How many items does this row show?

misconceptions.message: 3 × 20 = 60. A quarter symbol = 0.25 × 20 = 5. Total = 60 + 5 = 65.

bronze.display: In a grouped frequency table for heights, which class interval correctly includes the value 150 cm?

misconceptions.message: Standard class intervals use ≤ on the left and < on the right. 150 satisfies 150 ≤ h < 160 (it is the left boundary of this class, not the right boundary of the one before).

bronze.display: A frequency table shows 5 classes with frequencies 3, 7, 11, 8, and 1. What is the modal class frequency?

misconceptions.message: The modal class is the one with the highest frequency. Here that is 11. Do not give the class label — the question asks for the frequency value.

bronze.display: A frequency table for favourite sports has 5 rows. The total of all frequencies is 60. Three rows show 18, 12, and 9. The fourth row shows 14. What is the fifth frequency?

misconceptions.message: Sum the known frequencies: 18 + 12 + 9 + 14 = 53. Missing = 60 − 53 = 7.

silver.display: A pictogram shows daily visitors to a museum over 4 days. The key is 1 symbol = 50 visitors. Monday: 3 symbols; Tuesday: 4.5 symbols; Wednesday: 2 symbols; Thursday: 3.5 symbols. How many more visitors came on Tuesday than on Wednesday?

misconceptions.message: Tuesday: 4.5 × 50 = 225. Wednesday: 2 × 50 = 100. Difference = 225 − 100 = 125.
Apply the key to both rows before subtracting. Don’t subtract the symbol counts (4.5 − 2 = 2.5) then multiply — this gives a different error.

silver.display: A grouped frequency table for journey times shows: 0–10 min: 6; 10–20 min: 18; 20–30 min: f; 30–40 min: 9. The total number of journeys is 50. Find f.

A bar chart has its y-axis starting at 50 instead of 0. The bar for Group A reaches 80 and Group B reaches 100. A reporter claims Group B scored twice as many as Group A. Is this claim correct? Choose the best response.
options: Yes, because the bar for B is visually taller
No, because the true values are 80 and 100, a ratio of 4:5
Yes, because 100 is double 50
No, because both groups scored the same

misconceptions.message: True values are read from zero: 80 and 100. The ratio is 80:100 = 4:5, not 1:2. The truncated axis creates a visual illusion.

silver.display: A pictogram for rainfall has the key: 1 raindrop = 5 mm. A month shows 7 complete raindrops. A student draws a pictogram for a different month with 45 mm of rainfall. How many complete symbols should they draw?

misconceptions.message: Number of symbols = 45 ÷ 5 = 9. Check the value is an exact multiple of the key before drawing complete symbols only.

silver.display: Which of these is NOT an example of graphical misrepresentation?
options: A bar chart with the y-axis starting at 30 rather than 0
A pictogram where each symbol represents a different number in different rows
A frequency table listing every class interval with equal width
A chart where the bars for larger categories are drawn physically wider

misconceptions.message: A frequency table with equal-width classes is correctly constructed. Options A, B and D all describe specific types of misrepresentation (truncated axis, inconsistent key, distorted sizing).

silver.display: A tally chart records the shoe sizes of 30 students. After tallying, the frequencies are: size 5: 4; size 6: 9; size 7: 10; size 8: f; size 9: 2. Find f.

gold.display: A pictogram shows monthly sales for two products. Product A: 3.5 symbols (key: 1 symbol = 200 units). Product B: 2.25 symbols (key: 1 symbol = 400 units). How many more units did Product A sell than Product B?

misconceptions.message: Product A: 3.5 × 200 = 700. Product B: 2.25 × 400 = 900. Product A sold 200 fewer units (700 − 900 = −200, so B outsold A by 200). Check: different products use different keys here — you cannot compare symbol counts directly.
Each product row has its own key in this two-key pictogram. Apply the correct key to each row before comparing.

gold.display: A grouped frequency table for exam scores (out of 80) is shown. The classes are 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80 with frequencies 2, 8, 22, 18. Which statement correctly describes why a pictogram would NOT be an appropriate format for this data?
options: Pictograms can only show up to 4 categories
The frequencies are not exact multiples of a simple key value, making symbols hard to draw accurately
Pictograms cannot show grouped numerical data
The total frequency is too large for a pictogram

misconceptions.message: Pictograms work best when frequencies are whole multiples of the key. Here the total is 50, and frequencies like 22 and 18 don’t divide neatly into simple symbols. The format justification must refer to the data’s properties.

gold.display: A frequency table for the length of phone calls (in minutes) has classes 0–5, 5–10, 10–15, 15–20. The frequencies are 14, 26, 19, and 11. A data error is suspected: the original tally had a total of 72, but the table shows a total of 70. In which class is it most likely a tally bundle of 5 was miscounted as 3?
options: 0–5 (frequency 14)
5–10 (frequency 26)
10–15 (frequency 19)
15–20 (frequency 11)

misconceptions.message: The table total is 70 but should be 72, a shortfall of 2. If a bundle of 5 tally marks was misread as 3, exactly 2 marks are missing. The largest frequency (26, in class 5–10) has the most tally bundles and is most likely to contain this kind of counting error.

gold.display: A pictogram showing the number of passengers on four train routes uses symbols of different sizes: routes with more passengers have bigger symbols. Even so, each symbol still represents the same number. Explain whether this pictogram has a misrepresentation error.
options: No misrepresentation — as long as the key is the same, symbol size doesn’t matter
Yes — varying symbol sizes create distorted sizing, misleading readers about relative frequencies
Yes — pictograms must always use exactly 10 symbols per row
No misrepresentation — larger symbols just make the chart easier to read

misconceptions.message: Distorted sizing is a recognised form of graphical misrepresentation. Even if the key is constant, varying symbol sizes cause readers to perceive area differences rather than counting differences, exaggerating the apparent spread between categories.

gold.display: A frequency table records the number of goals scored per match for a football team over 38 matches: 0 goals: 8 matches; 1 goal: 12 matches; 2 goals: 9 matches; 3 goals: 6 matches; 4 or more goals: 3 matches. What fraction of matches saw the team score at least 2 goals? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

misconceptions.message: At least 2 goals means 2, 3, or 4+: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18 matches. Total = 38. Fraction = 18/38 = 9/19.
Include the ‘4 or more goals’ row in your count — ‘at least 2’ includes all classes from 2 onwards.
